props.title: The Armstrong Lie

sections.content: **The Armstrong Lie (2013)** (2013) started as a comeback story but transformed into something far darker. Director Alex Gibney originally set out to document Lance Armstrong's 2009 Tour de France return, similar to the triumphant tone of **Hoop Dreams** (1994). Instead, he captured the unraveling of sports' biggest deception. The film shares DNA with other sports documentaries that evolved mid-production like Icarus (2017), where Bryan Fogel accidentally documented the Russian Olympic doping scandal. Gibney's access becomes increasingly fascinating as Armstrong's carefully constructed narrative crumbles.

sections.content: The film exemplifies how sports documentaries evolved beyond simple hero worship. Like **Senna** (2010) and **When We Were Kings** (1996), it digs beneath surface mythology to examine the psychological complexity of elite athletes. Gibney's previous work exposing corruption in **Enron: The Smartest Guys in the Room** (2005) prepared him to dissect Armstrong's elaborate deception network. The documentary becomes a study in power, pride, and the lengths people will go to protect a profitable lie.

What sets **The Armstrong Lie** apart is its meta-narrative about documentary filmmaking itself. Like **Exit Through the Gift Shop** (2010) and **Capturing the Friedmans** (2003), the film's own production becomes part of the story. Gibney must confront how he was manipulated, turning his camera's gaze on the documentary process itself. Armstrong's careful image control and media manipulation are exposed through the filmmaker's personal journey from believer to skeptic. SUBHEAD: The Fall of Sports Heroes

movies.title: All the President's Men
movies.slug: The definitive film about investigative journalism exposing institutional corruption

sections.content: The film arrived during a period of increased scrutiny of sports icons, alongside revelations about Tiger Woods and Oscar Pistorius. Like **O.J.: Made in America** (2016), it examines how media and public hunger for inspiring narratives can enable corruption. Armstrong's cancer survival story, similar to the feel-good tone of **Brian's Song** (1971), made people resistant to questioning his success. The documentary shows how inspirational sports stories can become dangerous myths.
